source_text: Ποῦ τοίνυν ἐκεῖνο τὸ ὕδωρ; Δεικνύτωσαν ἡμῖν οἱ τὰ πάντα δεινοί. Ἆρ' οὐχὶ παντὶ δῆλον, ὅτι τῇ θερμότητι τοῦ ἡλίου διατμηθὲν ἀνηλώθη; Καίτοιγε οὐδὲ θερμὸν εἶναι τὸν ἥλιον ἐκεῖνοι λέγουσι· τοσοῦτον αὐτοῖς τοῦ λέγειν περίεστι. Καὶ σκοπεῖτε ποταπῇ ἀποδείξει ἐπερειδόμενοι πρὸς τὴν ἐνάργειαν ἀντιβαίνουσιν. Ἐπειδὴ λευκός ἐστι, φασὶ, τὴν χροίαν, ἀλλ' οὐχὶ ὑπέρυθρος, οὐδὲ ξανθὸς, τούτου ἕνεκεν οὐδὲ πυρώδης τὴν φύσιν· ἀλλὰ καὶ τούτου φασὶ τὸ θερμὸν ἐκ τῆς ταχείας εἶναι περιστροφῆς. Τί ἐντεῦθεν ἑαυτοῖς διοικούμενοι; Ὡς μηδὲν δόξαι τῶν ὑγρῶν ἀπαναλίσκειν τὸν ἥλιον. Ἐγὼ δὲ κἂν μὴ ἀληθὲς ᾖ τὸ λεγόμενον, ἀλλ' ὡς συγκατασκευάζον ἐμοὶ τὸν λόγον οὐκ ἀπωθοῦμαι. Ἐλέγετο γὰρ, διὰ τὴν ἐκ τοῦ θερμοῦ δαπάνην ἀναγκαῖον εἶναι τῶν ὑδάτων τὸ πλῆθος. Διαφέρει δὲ οὐδὲν, ἐκ φύσεως εἶναι θερμὸν, ἢ ἐκ πάθους ἔχειν τὴν πύρωσιν πρός γε τὸ τὰ αὐτὰ συμπτώματα περὶ τὰς αὐτὰς ὕλας ἀπογεννᾶν. Ἐάν τε γὰρ τριβόμενα ξύλα πρὸς ἄλληλα πῦρ καὶ φλόγα ἀνάψῃ, ἐάν τε ἐκ φλογὸς ἀναπτομένης κατακαυθῇ, ἴσον ἐστὶ καὶ παραπλήσιον ἐξ ἀμφοτέρων τὸ τέλος. Καίτοιγε ὁρῶμεν τὴν μεγάλην τοῦ τὰ πάντα κυβερνῶντος σοφίαν, μετατιθεῖσαν τὸν ἥλιον ἐξ ἑτέρων εἰς ἕτερα, ἵνα μὴ τοῖς αὐτοῖς ἀεὶ προσδιατρίβων, τῇ πλεονεξίᾳ τοῦ θερμοῦ λυμήνηται τὴν διακόσμησιν· ἀλλὰ νῦν μὲν αὐτὸν ἐπὶ τὸ νότιον μέρος κατὰ τὰς χειμερινὰς τροπὰς ἀπάγοντα, νῦν δὲ ἐπὶ τὰ ἰσημερινὰ σημεῖα μετατιθέντα, κἀκεῖθεν ἐπὶ τὰ προσάρκτια ὑπὸ τὰς θερινὰς τροπὰς ἐπανάγοντα, ὥστε τῇ κατὰ μικρὸν αὐτοῦ μεταβάσει τῷ περὶ γῆν τόπῳ τὴν εὐκρασίαν φυλάσ σεσθαι. Σκοπείτωσαν δὲ εἰ μὴ αὐτοὶ ἑαυτοῖς περιπίπτουσιν, οἵ γε τὴν θάλασσαν λέγουσι μήτε πλημμυρεῖν τοῖς ποταμοῖς ἐκ τῆς τοῦ ἡλίου δαπάνης, καὶ προσέτι ἁλμυρὰν καὶ πικρὰν ἀπολείπεσθαι, τοῦ λεπτοῦ καὶ ποτίμου ὑπὸ τῆς θέρμης ἀναλωθέντος· ὅπερ ἐκ τῆς τοῦ ἡλίου μάλιστα γίνεται διακρίσεως, τὸ μὲν κοῦφον ἀπάγοντος, τὸ δὲ παχὺ καὶ γεῶδες οἷόν τινα ἰλὺν καὶ ὑποστάθμην ἐναφιέντος· ἐξ οὗ τὸ πικρὸν καὶ ἁλμυρὸν καὶ ξηραντικὸν τῇ θαλάσσῃ προσεῖναι. Οἱ δὴ ταῦτα περὶ θαλάσσης λέγοντες, πάλιν μεταβαλλόμενοι, μηδεμίαν τοῦ ὑγροῦ γίνεσθαι μείωσιν ἐκ τοῦ ἡλίου φασί. 3.8 Καὶ ἐκάλεσεν ὁ Θεὸς τὸ στερέωμα οὐρανόν· ὡς κυρίως μὲν ἑτέρῳ τῆς προσηγορίας ἐφαρμοζούσης, καθ' ὁμοίωσιν δὲ καὶ τούτου μεταλαμβάνοντος τῆς κλήσεως. Τετηρήκαμεν δὲ πολλαχοῦ τὸν ὁρώμενον τόπον οὐρανὸν λεγόμενον (διὰ τὸ ναστὸν καὶ συνεχὲς τοῦ ἀέρος ἐναργῶς ἡμῶν ταῖς ὄψεσιν ὑποπίπτοντος, καὶ παρὰ τὸ ὁρᾶσθαι τῆς τοῦ οὐρανοῦ προσηγορίας ἀξιουμένου) ἐν οἷς φησι, Τὰ πετεινὰ τοῦ οὐρανοῦ. Καὶ πάλιν· Τὰ πετόμενα κατὰ τὸ στερέωμα τοῦ οὐρανοῦ. Τοιοῦτόν ἐστι καὶ τὸ, Ἀναβαίνουσιν ἕως τῶν οὐρανῶν. Καὶ Μωϋσῆς εὐλογῶν τὴν φυλὴν τοῦ Ἰωσὴφ, ἀπὸ ὡρῶν οὐρανοῦ, καὶ δρόσου, καὶ ἀπὸ ἡλίου τροπῶν, καὶ συνόδων μηνῶν, καὶ ἀπὸ κορυφῆς ὀρέων καὶ βουνῶν ἀεννάων τὰς εὐλογίας δίδωσιν, ὡς τοῦ περὶ γῆν τόπου διὰ τῆς ἐν τούτοις εὐταξίας εὐθηνουμένου. Ἀλλὰ καὶ ἐν ταῖς κατάραις τῷ Ἰσραὴλ, Ἔσται σοι, φησὶν, ὁ ὑπὲρ κεφαλῆς οὐρανὸς χαλκοῦς.
thought_title: The sun's heat and the naming of the firmament
orientation: Basil is answering opponents who deny that the sun is hot, then turns to the naming of the firmament as heaven.
pass_a_gloss: Where then is that water? Let those who are clever in all things show us. Is it not clear to everyone, that it was cut through by the heat of the sun and used up? And yet those men say that the sun is not even hot; so much surplus of speaking is theirs. And observe with what kind of proof they rely on when they resist the evidence. Since it is white, they say, in color, but not reddish, nor yellow, for this reason it is not fiery in nature; but they say that its heat is from the rapid rotation. What do they arrange for themselves from this? So that the sun may seem to consume none of the moist things. But I, even if the saying is not true, yet as it helps to build my argument I do not reject it. For it was being said, that because of the expenditure from the hot thing the abundance of waters was necessary. And it makes no difference, whether it is hot from nature, or has the burning from an affection, at least for producing the same results upon the same materials. For whether rubbed pieces of wood against each other kindle fire and flame, or whether they are burned up from a flame being kindled, the end from both is equal and similar. And yet we see the great wisdom of the one who governs all things, moving the sun from one place to another, so that not always lingering upon the same places, by the excess of heat it may harm the order; but now leading it to the southern part at the winter solstices, now moving it to the equinoctial points, and from there bringing it back to the northern parts at the summer solstices, so that by its gradual change the good temperature of the region around the earth may be preserved. But let them consider whether they do not fall upon themselves, those who say that the sea is not flooded by the rivers because of the expenditure of the sun, and moreover that it is left salty and bitter, the fine and drinkable part having been used up by the heat; which thing happens especially from the sun's separation, carrying off the light part, and leaving behind the thick and earthy part like some mud and sediment; from which the bitter and salty and drying quality belongs to the sea. Those who say these things about the sea, again changing, say that no diminution of the moist comes from the sun. And God called the firmament heaven: as the name properly belongs to another, but by likeness this also shares in the calling. And we have observed in many places the visible region being called heaven (because the solid and continuous air clearly falls under our sight, and because of being seen it is deemed worthy of the name of heaven) in which places it says, The birds of heaven. And again: The things flying across the firmament of heaven. Such also is the saying, They go up to the heavens. And Moses blessing the tribe of Joseph, from the seasons of heaven, and dew, and from the turnings of the sun, and the meetings of months, and from the top of mountains and everlasting hills gives the blessings, as the region around the earth being made fruitful through the good order in these things. But also in the curses to Israel, The heaven over your head, he says, will be bronze.

choices.english: those who are clever in all things
choices.why: Ironically renders the opponents' self-presentation as universal experts; keeps the sarcastic tone.

choices.english: was cut through and used up
choices.why: Preserves the two-step process: division by heat, then consumption.

choices.english: so much surplus of speaking is theirs
choices.why: Keeps the ironic 'surplus' metaphor for their excessive talk.
rejected: they have so much to say

choices.english: has the burning from an affection
choices.why: Retains the philosophical term 'affection' for an acquired quality, contrasting with nature.
Renders πλεονεξία as 'excess' in this physical context, not its usual moral sense of greed.
Keeps both terms for the residue left after evaporation, preserving the simile.

pass_b_english: Where then is that water? Let those who are clever in all things show us. Is it not obvious to everyone that it was cut through by the heat of the sun and used up? And yet those same people say the sun is not even hot—so much surplus of speaking is theirs. Consider what kind of proof they rely on when they oppose what is plainly evident. Because the sun is white in color, they say, and not reddish or yellow, for this reason it is not fiery in nature; but its heat, they say, comes from its rapid rotation. What do they gain for themselves by this? That the sun should not seem to consume any of the waters. For my part, even if what they say is not true, I do not reject it, since it helps to build my argument. For it was said that the abundance of waters was necessary because of the consumption caused by heat. And it makes no difference whether the sun is hot by nature or has its burning from an acquired condition, at least as far as producing the same results in the same materials. For whether wood rubbed together kindles fire and flame, or whether it is burned up by a kindled flame, the end from both is equal and alike. And indeed we see the great wisdom of him who governs all things, moving the sun from one region to another, so that by not always lingering upon the same places it may not damage the ordered arrangement by the excess of heat; but now he leads it toward the southern region at the winter solstice, now moves it to the equinoctial points, and from there brings it back toward the north at the summer solstice, so that by its gradual movement the good temperature of the region around the earth may be preserved. Let them consider whether they do not contradict themselves—they who say that the sea is not made to overflow by the rivers because of the sun's consumption, and moreover that it is left salty and bitter because the fine and drinkable part is used up by the heat; which happens especially from the separation accomplished by the sun, drawing off the light part and causing the thick and earthy part to settle like some mud and sediment; from this the bitter and salty and drying quality belongs to the sea. Those who say these things about the sea, turning around again, say that no diminution of moisture comes from the sun. And God called the firmament heaven (Genesis 1:8)—the name properly belongs to another, but this also shares in the title by way of likeness. We have observed that in many places the visible region is called heaven, because the solid and continuous air clearly falls under our sight, and because it is seen it is deemed worthy of the name of heaven; as in the words, The birds of heaven (Genesis 1:26). And again: The things that fly across the firmament of heaven (Genesis 1:20). Of this kind also is the saying, They go up to the heavens. And Moses, blessing the tribe of Joseph, gives blessings from the seasons of heaven and the dew, and from the sun's turnings and the meetings of months, and from the tops of mountains and everlasting hills (Deuteronomy 33:13-15), since the region around the earth is made fruitful through the good order in these things. But also in the curses upon Israel he says, The heaven over your head shall be bronze (Deuteronomy 28:23).

problems.source_quote: τῆς τοῦ ἡλίου μάλιστα γίνεται διακρίσεως
problems.why: διακρίσεως here means 'separation/distinction' in the sense of the sun's power to separate/filter, not 'the sun's separation' as if the sun itself is separated
problems.fix: the separation accomplished by the sun

edits.old: which happens especially from the sun's separation, drawing off the light part
edits.new: which happens especially from the separation accomplished by the sun, drawing off the light part

fixed: Changed 'the sun's separation' to 'the separation accomplished by the sun' because the source 'τῆς τοῦ ἡλίου μάλιστα γίνεται διακρίσεως' means the separation/filtering performed by the sun, not a separation of the sun itself.

problems.quote: the sea is not flooded by the rivers because of the sun's consumption
problems.source_quote: τὴν θάλασσαν λέγουσι μήτε πλημμυρεῖν τοῖς ποταμοῖς ἐκ τῆς τοῦ ἡλίου δαπάνης
problems.why: Source says sea is NOT flooded BY rivers; English says not flooded because of sun's consumption, dropping the agent.
problems.fix: the sea is not made to overflow by the rivers because of the sun's consumption
problems.ruling: Source: μήτε πλημμυρεῖν τοῖς ποταμοῖς = 'not flooded BY the rivers'; English misattributes agency to sun's consumption instead.

edits.old: the sea is not flooded by the rivers because of the sun's consumption
edits.new: the sea is not made to overflow by the rivers because of the sun's consumption

fixed: The English 'the sea is not flooded by the rivers because of the sun's consumption' does misstate the source. The source says the sea is not flooded BY the rivers (πλημμυρεῖν τοῖς ποταμοῖς), and the English drops the agent 'by the rivers'. The suggested fix 'the sea is not made to overflow by the rivers because of the sun's consumption' restores the agent and fits the sentence.

problems.why: ἐναφιέντος means 'sending in/letting sink in/infusing', not 'leaving behind'; sun causes thick part to settle in sea.
problems.ruling: ἐναφιέντος means 'sending in/infusing', opposite of 'leaving behind'; meaning reversed.

problems.source_quote: Τὰ πετεινὰ τοῦ οὐρανοῦ... Τὰ πετόμενα κατὰ τὸ στερέωμα τοὐ οὐρανοῦ
problems.why: First 'birds of heaven' is Genesis 1:26 or 2:19, not 1:20; second 'flying across firmament' is 1:20. Citation wrong for first.
problems.ruling: First citation 'Genesis 1:20' wrong; Τὰ πετεινὰ τοῦ οὐρανοῦ is from Matthew 13:32, not Genesis.

edits.old: leaving behind the thick and earthy part
edits.new: causing the thick and earthy part to settle

fixed: ἐναφιέντος means 'sending in/letting sink in', so 'leaving behind' misstates the source; changed to 'causing the thick and earthy part to settle'.
The first 'birds of heaven' is not Genesis 1:20; changed citation to Genesis 1:26.

dismissed.why: Citation should be Genesis 1:26 LXX, but birds appear on day 5 (Gen 1:20-21); 1:26 mentions birds but 'according to their kinds'. Better: Genesis 1:20 or 1:21.
dismissed.note: LXX Genesis 1:26 does contain τῶν πετεινῶν τοῦ οὐρανοῦ, so the citation is acceptable.
